title: Hilbert 14: The Alternating Group Aₙ and the Vandermonde Invariant
description: The parent chain (hilbert-14-oq-02, hilbert-14-oq-02-oq-01) pins the optimal degree bound β(Sₙ) = n for the SYMMETRIC group Sₙ: its invariant ring is R[e₁,…,eₙ]. This entry addresses the OQ-02 follow-up 'identify the generating invariants and their degrees for another classical group' for the ALTERNATING group Aₙ ⊆ Sₙ. The new phenomenon is the Vandermonde/discriminant polynomial Δ = ∏_{i<j}(xⱼ - xᵢ), the prototypical ALTERNATING invariant. Main results, all 0-axiom: (1) Δ is alternating — rename e Δ = sign(e) • Δ for every permutation e, proved by evaluating on all points (MvPolynomial.funext) and reducing to the classical determinant fact that permuting the rows of a Vandermonde matrix scales its determinant by the sign (Matrix.det_permute + Matrix.det_vandermonde); (2) Δ is an Aₙ-invariant — every even permutation fixes it; (3) over an infinite integral domain with 2 ≠ 0 and n ≥ 2, Δ is NOT symmetric, hence Δ ∉ R[e₁,…,eₙ]: a genuinely new generator absent from the Sₙ-invariants; (4) Δ² IS symmetric (the discriminant lies in R[e₁,…,eₙ]), so Δ is a square root of a symmetric polynomial — the defining relation of Aₙ-invariants over Sₙ-invariants; (5) Δ is homogeneous of degree ∑_i |{j : i<j}| = C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2, the degree of the new alternating generator. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

meta.assumptions: None. All theorems fully proved with 0 axioms and 0 sorries (no native_decide; only decide-free tactics). #print axioms reports only [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] for the alternating law, non-membership, Δ²-symmetry and the degree formula. The alternating law, Aₙ-invariance and Δ²-symmetry are stated over an infinite integral domain R (the standard hypothesis of MvPolynomial.funext); the non-symmetry / non-membership results additionally require 2 ≠ 0 and n ≥ 2 (necessarily: in characteristic 2, alternating = symmetric and Δ is symmetric; for n < 2 there are no pairs and Δ = 1). SCOPE: this identifies the new generating invariant of the alternating group (the discriminant Δ) and its degree, and proves it is absent from the symmetric-group invariants R[e₁,…,eₙ]. It does NOT prove that R[x]^{Aₙ} = R[e₁,…,eₙ][Δ] as a full generation statement (a separate, longer development); the entry establishes the distinguishing generator and its algebraic relation Δ² ∈ R[e₁,…,eₙ].

overview.historicalContext: Hilbert's 14th problem concerns finite generation of invariant rings R[V]^G, and a natural refinement (the parent OQ-02) asks for the OPTIMAL degree bound β(G) together with an explicit generating set. For the symmetric group Sₙ the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Polynomials gives the clean answer: R[x₁,…,xₙ]^{Sₙ} = R[e₁,…,eₙ] with eₖ of degree k, so β(Sₙ) = n. The very next classical group is the alternating group Aₙ ⊆ Sₙ of even permutations. Classically its invariant ring is R[e₁,…,eₙ][Δ] where Δ = ∏_{i<j}(xⱼ - xᵢ) is the Vandermonde/discriminant polynomial: Δ is the prototypical ALTERNATING function, picking up the sign of the permutation, so it is fixed by the even permutations but not by odd ones, and Δ² (the discriminant) is symmetric. Thus Aₙ needs exactly one new generator beyond the elementary symmetric polynomials, of degree n(n-1)/2 — far larger than β(Sₙ) = n. This entry formalizes the key structural facts about this new generator.
overview.problemStatement: For the alternating group Aₙ acting on R[x₁,…,xₙ], identify and characterize the generating invariant that distinguishes R[x]^{Aₙ} from the symmetric invariants R[e₁,…,eₙ]: the Vandermonde polynomial Δ = ∏_{i<j}(xⱼ - xᵢ). Prove (i) Δ is alternating (rename e Δ = sign(e) • Δ), so it is an Aₙ-invariant; (ii) over an infinite integral domain with 2 ≠ 0 and n ≥ 2, Δ is not symmetric, hence Δ ∉ R[e₁,…,eₙ]; (iii) Δ² is symmetric; (iv) Δ is homogeneous of degree n(n-1)/2.
overview.proofStrategy: The technical heart is proving the alternating law rename e Δ = sign(e) • Δ WITHOUT any hand computation of how a permutation reorders the product over pairs. Instead work through evaluation: (1) eval_vandermondePoly shows eval v Δ = det (vandermonde v) (eval is a ring hom, so it distributes over the double product, matching det_vandermonde's formula ∏_i ∏_{j∈Ioi i}(v j - v i)); (2) vandermonde_comp_perm shows vandermonde (v ∘ e) = (vandermonde v).submatrix e id (a row permutation, entrywise by rfl); (3) eval_rename_vandermondePoly combines eval_rename with det_permute to get eval v (rename e Δ) = sign(e) • eval v Δ for every point v; (4) MvPolynomial.funext (valid over an infinite integral domain) upgrades this pointwise identity to the polynomial identity rename e Δ = sign(e) • Δ. From the alternating law everything follows: Aₙ-invariance is the sign = 1 case; Δ²-symmetry is sign² = 1; and non-symmetry uses a transposition (sign = -1) evaluated at an injective tuple, where the Vandermonde determinant is nonzero (det_vandermonde_ne_zero_iff), so -x = x forces 2x = 0 and, with 2 ≠ 0 in a domain, a contradiction. Homogeneity is a product of C(n,2) degree-one factors (IsHomogeneous.prod), and the degree sum ∑_i |Ioi i| collapses to n(n-1)/2 by a Gauss-sum reflection.
keyInsights: The alternating law rename e Δ = sign(e) • Δ — normally proved by tracking how a permutation reorders the factors of ∏_{i<j}(xⱼ-xᵢ) — is obtained for free by evaluating on all points and invoking the Vandermonde determinant's row-permutation behaviour (det_permute), then using MvPolynomial.funext. This trades a delicate combinatorial argument for two off-the-shelf lemmas.

Δ is the single new generator that separates the Aₙ-invariants from the Sₙ-invariants: it is fixed by even permutations (Aₙ-invariant) but changes sign under odd ones (not Sₙ-invariant), so R[x]^{Aₙ} strictly contains R[e₁,…,eₙ].

The characteristic hypothesis 2 ≠ 0 is essential, not cosmetic: in characteristic 2 the sign is trivial (−1 = 1), alternating collapses to symmetric, and Δ IS symmetric. The proof isolates exactly this dependence (the step −x = x ⟹ x = 0).

Δ² is symmetric because sign² = 1 — this is the algebraic relation defining the Aₙ-invariants as a degree-two extension of the Sₙ-invariants: R[x]^{Aₙ} = R[e₁,…,eₙ][Δ] with Δ² ∈ R[e₁,…,eₙ] equal to the discriminant.

The degree of the new generator is n(n-1)/2 = C(n,2), the number of pairs i < j — vastly larger than the symmetric bound β(Sₙ) = n, showing how sharply the optimal degree can jump between a group and an index-two subgroup.
prerequisites: Symmetric and alternating polynomials; the Sₙ-action by renaming variables
Vandermonde matrix and determinant; permutation sign and det_permute
MvPolynomial evaluation as a ring homomorphism and MvPolynomial.funext over infinite domains
Homogeneous polynomials and the Gauss sum ∑ i = n(n-1)/2

sections.title: Header: The Vandermonde Invariant for the Alternating Group
sections.summary: States the follow-up question this file addresses — the parent chain settles the optimal degree bound β(Sₙ)=n for the symmetric group's invariant ring R[e₁,…,eₙ]; this entry identifies the generating invariant for the alternating group Aₙ ⊆ Sₙ, namely the Vandermonde/discriminant polynomial Δ = ∏_{i<j}(xⱼ−xᵢ). It proves Δ is alternating (rename e Δ = sign(e)•Δ, via MvPolynomial.funext and the classical fact that permuting Vandermonde matrix rows scales the determinant by the sign), hence Aₙ-invariant but not Sₙ-invariant (so Δ ∉ R[e₁,…,eₙ], a genuinely new generator), while Δ² is symmetric — the algebraic relation Aₙ-invariants satisfy over the Sₙ-invariants — and Δ is homogeneous of degree C(n,2).
sections.mathContext: $\Delta = \prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)$ satisfies $\mathrm{rename}\,e\,\Delta = \mathrm{sign}(e)\cdot\Delta$; $\Delta$ generates the $A_n$-invariants beyond $R[e_1,\dots,e_n]$, with $\Delta^2$ symmetric and $\deg\Delta = \binom{n}{2}$.

conclusion.summary: For the alternating group Aₙ ⊆ Sₙ, the Vandermonde/discriminant polynomial Δ = ∏_{i<j}(xⱼ - xᵢ) is the generating invariant that distinguishes R[x]^{Aₙ} from the symmetric invariants R[e₁,…,eₙ]. This entry proves, with 0 axioms and 0 sorries: Δ is alternating (rename e Δ = sign(e) • Δ), hence an Aₙ-invariant; over an infinite integral domain with 2 ≠ 0 and n ≥ 2 it is not symmetric, so Δ ∉ R[e₁,…,eₙ]; Δ² is symmetric (Δ is a square root of a symmetric polynomial); and Δ is homogeneous of degree n(n-1)/2 = C(n,2).
conclusion.implications: The proof introduces a reusable technique: the alternating law of Δ — classically an exercise in tracking how a permutation reorders a product over pairs — is obtained by evaluating on all points and reducing to the Vandermonde determinant's row-permutation behaviour (Matrix.det_permute), then invoking MvPolynomial.funext. This eval+funext route sidesteps combinatorial sign bookkeeping entirely and applies to any polynomial identity that can be certified pointwise. Mathematically, the entry exhibits how sharply the optimal degree β(G) can change between a group and an index-two subgroup: β(Sₙ) = n but Aₙ needs a generator of degree n(n-1)/2. It also formalizes the degree-two relation Δ² ∈ R[e₁,…,eₙ] that presents the Aₙ-invariants as R[e₁,…,eₙ][Δ] modulo Δ² = discriminant.
openQuestions: Prove the full generation statement R[x₁,…,xₙ]^{Aₙ} = R[e₁,…,eₙ][Δ] (that the elementary symmetric polynomials together with Δ generate ALL Aₙ-invariants), realizing the invariant ring explicitly as a free rank-two module over R[e₁,…,eₙ] with basis {1, Δ}.
Express Δ² as an explicit polynomial in e₁,…,eₙ (the discriminant as a symmetric function), giving the defining relation of the extension R[e₁,…,eₙ] ⊆ R[e₁,…,eₙ][Δ] in closed form.

Extend the eval+funext technique to compute generating invariants and degrees for further classical groups (e.g. signed-permutation / hyperoctahedral groups Bₙ, Dₙ), where Mathlib's determinant and Pfaffian machinery can supply the pointwise identities.
